subject: armadillo
pitch: A nine-banded armadillo trotting along. A shell of overlapping banded plates in dusty pinkish-tan, a pointy snout, tall leathery ears, small beady eyes, sturdy clawed feet and a long armoured tail tapering to a point. A sprinkle of coarse pale hairs pokes out between the bands.
reasoning:
I'm planning a stylized low-poly three.js armadillo module, sizing it realistically at roughly 0.9m total length with tail, 0.25m shoulder height, and about 0.55m body length from head to rump.

I'm figuring out how to construct the segmented carapace shell with its scapular shield, nine movable bands, and pelvic shield, considering using sliced sphere or cylinder geometries with arc segments to create the banded dome effect along the body.

Working out sphere polar axis math to orient bands along Z...

This rotation math is getting messy, so I think it's cleaner to write my own procedural geometry generator instead — a parametric surface function covering just the upper half of a banded shell, with separate meshes for each band to create the gaps I need.

Now I'm sketching the overall body shape: width and height profiles along the length, with a shield at the shoulders, banded midsection, and a rounded pelvic shield at the rear. I'm working out realistic dimensions for a nine-banded armadillo — roughly 0.5m body length, 0.38m tail, shoulder height around 0.15-0.18m, and shell width near 0.22m.

I'm positioning the body along z with the head toward the front and tail trailing behind, setting leg height so the shell sits a bit above the ground, and modeling the shell itself as the upper half of an ellipsoid that meets a softer, paler belly region underneath — since the shell covers the top and sides but the underside is soft and hairy, not armored.

I'm working out a cross-sectional parametrization where the shell's width and height taper smoothly toward the front and back, closing off naturally at the head and tail ends, with the shell bands only covering the upper arc so the belly stays separate below.

Now I'm planning the shield-and-band layout: a front scapular shield, nine shell bands with small gaps, and a rear pelvic shield. I'm also considering a canvas-based texture for the shell surface to give it a dusty pinkish-tan speckled look with subtle pits and grain, though I'm weighing whether relying on canvas/DOM texture generation is appropriate for this environment.

For the coarse pale hairs poking from the band gaps, I'm thinking around 60 small thin cone or cylinder meshes sharing geometry, kept simple rather than instanced or merged. For the ears, I'm picturing tall leathery rounded-triangular shapes using a flattened cone with a darker pinkish-grey material.

For the head I'm shaping it as a shield-like form tapering into a pointy snout, built from a flattened ellipsoid body plus a tapered cylinder rotated along the Z axis so the narrow end forms the snout tip, with further scaling to flatten and narrow it properly.

I'm positioning the head forward and slightly down from the shell at roughly z 0.31-0.52, giving it a slight downward pitch for a natural trotting posture, and adding a small darker nose tip plus tiny beady eye spheres embedded on either side near the snout base.

For ears, I'm placing small flattened teardrop-like shapes near the top-back of the head on each side, tilted outward and upward, using a stretched sphere or cone geometry with a leathery pinkish-grey material for that tough, rounded armadillo ear look.

Now I'm working out leg placement for a diagonal trotting gait, with front legs near the front of the shell and back legs farther back, planning sturdy clawed feet with the diagonal pairs swinging together.

Writing leg geometry...

That looks like a trot mid-stride, so I should add a knee/elbow bend to the lower legs for a more natural fold, keeping it modest since armadillos have short legs. For the tail, I'm planning a tapering series of 10-12 frustum segments with decreasing radii from base to tip, curving slightly downward from the shell toward the ground to mimic the banded, armoured look.

Now I'm working out how to orient each tail segment along its curve using a quaternion to align with the tangent direction, plus adding small coarse hairs poking out between the shell's band gaps—placing them via surface normals computed from the shell's parametric shape with slight random jitter for a natural, scruffy look.

I need to figure out the shell's cross-section curve from front to back, using a power function of sine for a blunt rear and rounded front, but I'm running into a singularity issue where the surface normal becomes undefined exactly at the poles since the tangent vectors collapse there.

I'll clamp the parameter range to avoid the exact poles, accepting that the front shield naturally tapers since the head emerges from that area anyway. For the cross-section I'm keeping width and height scaled by this shape function with an offset center height to match where the dome sits above the legs, checking that the bottom edge roughly aligns with the top of the legs.

For the actual shell shape, I want something flatter and boxier than a pure ellipse, so I'm switching to a superellipse cross-section using a power function that squares off the cosine and sine terms—giving that distinctive armadillo plating look rather than a smooth dome. I still need to work out how the belly-side portion of this cross-section closes up properly at the bottom.

Now I'm figuring out how to divide the body length along the arc into the scapular shield up front, nine narrow bands in the middle, and the pelvic shield at the rear, trying to allocate reasonable proportions in meters for each segment while accounting for the fact that uniform spacing in the angle parameter doesn't translate to uniform spacing in actual z-length near the body's ends.

For each band I want a tiling effect, like overlapping plates, so I'm thinking of giving each band a convex ridge by scaling its cross-section outward near the middle and tapering at the edges—simpler than computing true surface normals, and it should still read as armor segments with grooves between them.

To make the gaps between bands look believable, I'm adding a continuous darker inner shell underneath, slightly scaled down so it peeks through as shadow. Then each band becomes its own small grid mesh spanning the visible arc, with roughly a dozen bands plus shield patches total, using two alternating tan tones for the band coloring to add visual variety without overcomplicating the material count.

For extra richness, I'm thinking about adding a seeded-noise canvas texture to the shell surface—speckled pits and granular highlights mapped via UV coordinates along the band and around the cross-section—so the shell isn't just flat color. I'd use two slightly different tinted materials sharing the same texture map to vary band appearance while staying within a reasonable color budget.

Now I'm settling on the full color palette: dusty pinkish-tan shell and bands with a darker alt tone, a soft pale pink belly, grayish-pinkish scaly legs with cream claws, leathery pinkish-grey ears, dark eyes and nose, pale coarse cream hairs, and alternating banded tail rings—then starting to think through the trotting pose and body posture.

Now I'm working out the body geometry—computing where the belly ellipsoid sits relative to the shell's lower edge so the legs emerge naturally from the shell-belly junction without visibly clipping, using the parametric cross-section math to find exact y and x coordinates at the shell skirt.

Then I'm sizing the leg segments: hip pivot position, upper and lower leg cylinder lengths and radii, and foot pivot placement so the total leg reaches from hip to ground at y=0, keeping the low-slung armadillo stance realistic.

I'm working out the foot placement so the bottom touches the ground, accepting a tiny couple millimeters of sink as acceptable. I realize that when the leg rotates for the trot pose, the vertical extent shrinks by roughly cosθ, lifting the feet a few millimeters off the floor — which is actually fine since one diagonal pair should be raised during a trot, but I need to make sure the model still stands properly in the neutral pose.

Rather than trying to hand-compute exact offsets, I decide the robust approach is to compute the model's bounding box after construction and shift the whole group so its minimum y equals zero, making sure to update world matrices first so the rotated geometry is accounted for correctly.

I realize using the imprecise bounding-box option could overestimate the rotated leg geometry, letting feet float above the floor, so I should use the precise vertex-based bounding box instead — it's a bit costlier but manageable given the mesh count.

Then I turn to the trot pose and proportions: some legs lifting slightly is fine for a trotting stance, and the shell height, body length, and head placement all seem reasonably proportioned for a stylized armadillo, with the head shield sitting as a flattened dome slightly below the shell's top height.

Now I'm working out the snout geometry — a tapered cylinder rotated to point forward from the head sphere, flattened vertically and faceted with low-poly segments, with a small dark nose sphere at the tip to give it a pointy, low-poly armadillo snout shape.

For the head pitch, I'm setting up a rotation around the X axis so a positive angle tilts the nose downward, giving a slight forward-looking trotting posture — nesting the head, snout, and ears inside a headGroup pivoted at the neck so the rotation naturally carries all the head parts together.

Now I'm working out positions relative to that head group's local origin: the cranium as a small ellipsoid, the snout as a tapered cylinder nestled mostly inside it, and the eyes placed right on the cranium's surface using the ellipsoid equation to check they sit flush rather than floating or buried.

Working out the nose, ears, and highlights now — placing a small dark sphere at the snout tip for the nose, and figuring out tilted, scaled spheres for tall leathery ears positioned behind and above the cranium, including the rotation math needed to angle them outward and backward correctly.

I'll scale back the ear height to a more reasonable 5cm above the shell, still reading as tall and leathery. For orientation, I'm making the ear plate thin along X so its broad face reads from the side, scaled wider in Y and Z, then angling the ears outward and slightly forward with rotation on the Z and X axes.

I'm considering adding a lighter pink inner-ear layer for extra detail but will likely skip it to keep things simple—just one leathery outer ear mesh per side, darker grey-brown in color.

Now I'm working out the leg placement: front legs sit further forward and rear legs further back, with their x-position calculated so they tuck just inside the shell's width at that height, letting them emerge naturally from under the shell's edge. Each leg is built from nested pivot groups—hip, knee, ankle—with tapered cylinders for upper and lower leg segments and a small ellipsoid foot at the end, all positioned relative to their parent joint.

I'm now recalculating the leg segment lengths so the total hip-to-foot distance matches the hip height of 0.07, since my earlier dimensions were overshooting and pushing the feet too far below ground level, which would throw off the auto-grounding and shell positioning. I'm adjusting upper leg to 0.03, lower leg to 0.026, and the foot's bottom offset to 0.014 below the ankle so everything sums to exactly 0.07.

Now I'm thinking through the trot gait mechanics, specifically how the knee joint should bend during the forward swing -- the lower leg needs a counter-rotation relative to the upper leg so the paw lifts naturally as the diagonal leg pairs swing forward and back.

I'm also working out the claw placement on the feet: three small cones per foot, offset along x and positioned at the front edge, oriented to point forward and slightly downward to match the foot's local coordinate frame.

I'll write a helper function to place claw cones with shared geometry, colored cream, positioned at each toe tip. For the feet I'm planning 4 claws per foot spaced evenly across the front edge, calculating their x-offsets and z-position based on the foot ellipsoid's dimensions in the ankle-centered coordinate frame.

Structuring the leg hierarchy as nested groups -- hip, lower leg, foot -- each with cylinder/ellipsoid meshes and rotation pivots, I verify the total leg length sums correctly below the hip. I'm also considering adding small scute-like tubercle bumps and sparse hair texture to the shell beyond the main bands, then moving on to building the tail.

I'm positioning the tail base where the shell's rear cross-section narrows, embedding it near the shell surface, then defining a curved path for the tail that sags slightly over its length, roughly 0.4 units long compared to the 0.56 body length. I'm dividing the tail into 14 tapering segments, each a frustum with slightly protruding bony rings, radius shrinking toward a point at the tip.

I'm generating each ring as a short cylinder oriented along the tail curve, with alternating darker/lighter materials for the armored band effect and a tapered cone tip at the very end. Now I'm thinking about scattering small hair details at the gaps between the shell's armor bands.

I'll compute the normal using the cross product of partial derivatives with respect to z and t, checking orientation against the center axis, then work out the shell radius formula using a square-root sine profile to taper the cross-section toward the pointed front tip, testing a few z-values to confirm it stays reasonably blunt rather than collapsing too sharply.

I realize the profile simplifies nicely to `(1-(z/L)²)^0.25`, avoiding the acos entirely, giving a flattish middle with steep tapering at both ends, which fits an armadillo body well. Now I'm defining a band geometry function that builds grid vertices across a z-range and t-range, scaling width and height by this profile and adding an optional ridge bulge along the band.

Writing band geometry logic...

Now I'm worried about normal orientation -- whether the grid winding produces outward-facing normals or if I'll need to flip them or rely on double-sided shading to avoid dark faces.

I verify the second triangle (b,d,c) gives the same orientation as the first since both reduce to the cross product of the du and dt directions. To be extra safe, I could just rely on computeVertexNormals to derive consistent normals rather than hand-verifying each case.

The superellipse parameterization has vertical tangents at certain points, but since normals come from averaging adjacent triangles, this shouldn't cause visible artifacts. The inner dark base skin sits slightly under the outer shell at a smaller scale, so it's designed to peek through gaps between the bands rather than be fully covered.

I'm also working out the belly geometry — a soft pale pinkish ellipsoid positioned below center that should be mostly hidden by the shell but peek out at the underside between the legs, overlapping with where the dark base skin shows through at the skirt region.

For the skirt color where the base peeks between shell bands, I'm leaning toward a medium dusty brown-pink tone to suggest leathery exposed skin rather than a stark dark shadow line. For the head, I'm planning to reuse the shell's pinkish-tan material for the cranium sphere so it blends with the body, using a flat shield color for the snout.

Now I'm designing the texture-tinting approach: a single neutral grayish speckled canvas texture that gets tinted differently via material color for the shield, main bands, and alternate bands, giving variation without needing separate textures. Writing speckle dot generation...

Then I'm working out hair placement along the band gap boundaries, computing surface normals via finite differences and cross products to orient hair geometry correctly, and defining leg swing angles for a trot pose where diagonal legs alternate between forward-swing and stance positions, relying on auto-grounding to let the stance legs set the body height. I'm also sketching out the band and feet geometry builders, mesh counts for claws and bands, and a surface normal function to orient the hairs outward and slightly backward.

Now I'm detailing the shell construction—front and rear shield patches with degenerate tips, alternating band materials for visual rhythm, and an inner base shell slightly recessed to create dark gaps between bands. I'm placing the belly sphere and checking it doesn't clip through the leg hip attachment points, then moving to the head: cranium, snout cylinder rotated to point forward, nose, beady eyes with tiny highlights, and tall leaning ears built from scaled spheres with combined X/Z rotations to angle them outward and back.

I'm defining the tapering tail as a sequence of ringed cone segments that flare slightly at each base for an armored, stepped look, alternating two tail colors, with the final ring shrinking to a near-point tip. Finally I'm wrapping the whole build in a function that constructs the model, computes its bounding box, and shifts it vertically so the lowest point rests exactly on the floor.

I'm sketching out a seeded random number generator and a color palette for shell, bands, belly, legs, claws, eyes, nose, hair, and tail, then writing helper functions for materials and the shell's superellipse profile shape. I'm working out the exact z-boundaries between the nine bands plus front and rear shields, making sure each boundary leaves a small gap, and planning to scatter sparse pale hairs along those boundary gaps using thin tapered cylinders oriented outward from the shell surface with some random jitter in direction and length.

Writing hair placement code...

Now I'm designing the legs: tapered cylinders for upper and lower segments, a flattened ellipsoid for the foot, and small backward-rotated cones for claws, all assembled into hip/knee/ankle pivot groups so each leg can be posed with a swing and knee-bend rotation. I'm working out specific swing/knee angle values for a diagonal trot gait—front-left and rear-right forward together, front-right and rear-left back—checking the resulting foot height differences to make sure the lifted legs clear the ground believably.

For the tail, I'm building a tapered curve of short cylinder segments following a sagging path downward and backward from the body, alternating two tail-band colors, with each segment oriented via quaternion along its direction vector. Then I'm setting up the head group with a scaled sphere for the cranium using the same shell texture, plus eyes, nose, and ears to add later, and planning to ground the whole model by computing its bounding box and shifting it up so the feet touch y=0. I'm listing out all the materials needed (shield, bands, inner skin, belly, legs, claws, ears, eyes, nose, hair, tail colors) and double-checking that hair placement aligns with the band gaps where the bulge is zero, then starting to verify that the head's size and position proportionally cover the front of the shell without awkward overlap.

I'm reconsidering the overall body scale—realizing my initial proportions made the armadillo too long compared to a real nine-banded armadillo—so I'm recalculating the shell length, width, height, head position, snout dimensions, tail curve, and leg placements with smaller, more realistic values, then re-deriving where the ears, eyes, and tail base should sit relative to the new shell profile.
